title: Pronouns and respect
description: Say I, you, he, she, it, we and they, and choose the right level of respect.

guide.title: I, we and the two words for 'you'
guide.text:
ನಾನು (naanu) is 'I' and ನಾವು (naavu) is 'we'.

For 'you' there are two words. ನೀನು (neenu) is familiar: use it only with children, close friends of your own age, younger brothers and sisters - and people use it to God. ನೀವು (neevu) is polite, and is also the plural 'you all'. Use neevu with every adult you meet until they invite you to do otherwise; using neenu to a stranger, an elder or someone serving you is rude.

The verb changes to match: neenu takes endings in -eeya or the bare command form, neevu takes -eera and the polite command ending -i.

examples.english: You come. (to a child or friend)
Please come. (polite, or to several people)

guide.title: He, she and they: gender plus respect
guide.text:
The third person shows three things at once: near or far, male or female, and respect.

Far (that person): ಅವನು (avanu) he, ಅವಳು (avalu) she, ಅವರು (avaru) they. Near (this person here): ಇವನು (ivanu), ಇವಳು (ivalu), ಇವರು (ivaru). The first sound tells you: a- is 'that', i- is 'this'.

avanu and avalu are familiar, like neenu: use them for children, friends and younger relatives. For any adult you respect - parents, teachers, colleagues, strangers - use avaru, the plural, even for one person. The verb is then plural too: avaru iddaare, 'he/she is (here)'. Only context tells you whether avaru means 'he', 'she' or 'they'.

Respect matters more than gender here: a mother is avaru, not avalu.

guide.title: It and they for things: adu, idu, avu, ivu
guide.text:
Everything that is not a human being - objects, animals, ideas - is neuter in Kannada. There is no grammatical gender to memorise for nouns: a table is 'it', a dog is 'it'.

ಅದು (adu) is 'that, it' and ಇದು (idu) is 'this'. Their plurals are ಅವು (avu) 'those, they' and ಇವು (ivu) 'these'. A baby or small child is also often called adu, affectionately.

Neuter subjects take their own verb forms: adu ide (it is), avu ive (they are).

guide.title: Every pronoun has its own verb ending
guide.text:
Kannada verbs agree with the subject in person, number and - in the third person singular - gender. Here is 'to be (somewhere)' with each pronoun; the same endings appear on every verb in the language, so this table is worth learning by heart.

naanu iddeeni, neenu iddeeya, avanu iddaane, avalu iddaale, adu ide; naavu iddeevi, neevu iddeera, avaru iddaare, avu ive.

Notice the pattern: -eeni (I), -eeya (you familiar), -aane (he), -aale (she), -eevi (we), -eera (you polite), -aare (they / respectful he or she). The neuter forms ide and ive are the odd ones out.

examples.english: They are at home. / He or she is at home. (respectful)

phrases.english: Where are you? (to a friend or child)
phrases.note: neenu is familiar - never use it with elders or strangers.
avanu is fine for someone younger than you.
The l in avalu is the retroflex ಳ.
Equally 'She is my teacher': avaru does not show gender.
Could also mean 'He/She is my friend', said respectfully.

phrases.english: This is Ravi. (a boy or a friend)
phrases.note: For an adult you are introducing politely, say ivaru.

phrases.english: This is Geetha. (a girl or a friend)

phrases.note: -galu is the plural ending for things.

phrases.english: You come. (to a friend or child)
phrases.note: The bare verb is the familiar command.
The polite command of baa (come) is irregular: banni.
